label: Chapter 5: Neutrality, Iron and a New Dynasty, 1867 to 1914

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: The treaty of 1867 promised that the fortress would be taken apart.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And it kept its word. Over the next sixteen years, work crews tore down walls, filled in ditches, and blew up forts and bastions.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It was one of the biggest demolition projects in Europe.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Sixteen years of knocking things down.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And when it was done, a city that had been a cramped military stronghold for centuries was suddenly free to grow.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: What did it do with the space?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Parks, boulevards, and building plots.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: New districts spread across the plateau, and the deep valleys that had been obstacles became green spaces.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1903, the city opened the Adolphe Bridge, which sweeps across the Pétrusse valley in two graceful stone arches.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: At the time, it was one of the largest stone arch bridges in the world.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And not everything was destroyed.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Parts of the casemates survived, and so did the old town on its cliffs.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1994, UNESCO recognized the old quarters and the surviving fortifications as a World Heritage site.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The Gibraltar of the North had become, in the end, a beautiful ruin.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Okay. But the neutrality. That was a gamble, wasn't it?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A real one. The great powers had guaranteed it together, which in practice meant that if anyone broke it, no single power was obliged to punish them.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So it's a promise from everyone, which is a promise from nobody.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Pretty much. And the country had almost no army, only a small corps of volunteers and gendarmes.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Luxembourg's safety depended on the goodwill of its neighbors.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Not a great strategy.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Not a great strategy. But while the diplomats worried, something was happening underground.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Ooh. What?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In the south of Luxembourg, running down into the French region of Lorraine, there is a belt of iron ore called minette, a reddish-brown stone.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Local blacksmiths had known about it for centuries, but it was nearly useless, because it contained a lot of phosphorus, which made the iron brittle.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Until...

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Until 1878. That year, an Englishman named Sidney Gilchrist Thomas and his cousin Percy Gilchrist developed a way to remove the phosphorus.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Suddenly the poor ore of Luxembourg and Lorraine could be made into excellent steel.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So the worst rock in the country became the best one.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: An industrial revolution in miniature.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Blast furnaces went up along the Alzette and across the southwest corner of the country.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Villages like Esch, Differdange, Dudelange and Rumelange swelled into industrial towns.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The night sky over the south turned orange, and red dust settled on everything.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Red dust on everything. Lovely.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Within a generation, the country that had been exporting farmers to America was importing workers.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: From where?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: First from Germany, then from Italy.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Italian laborers began arriving in large numbers in the eighteen-nineties and settled in the steel towns.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: They were the first of many waves.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Luxembourg had a long tradition of sending its sons and daughters abroad.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Now, for the first time, it began to receive people.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the companies consolidated.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1911, the main steel producers merged into a single giant called ARBED, a name built from the French words for the united steelworks of Burbach, Eich and Dudelange.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Say that three times fast.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: For most of the twentieth century, ARBED was practically a state within the state.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Per head of population, few places in the world made more steel.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And who ran the country during all this?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A careful lawyer named Paul Eyschen, head of the government from 1888 until 1915.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: An extraordinary twenty-seven years.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: He guided Luxembourg through industrialization and the pressures of its neighbors.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Twenty-seven years. Imagine the paperwork.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Now, for the strangest episode.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The change of dynasty.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Oh, I've been waiting for this.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1890, King William the Third of the Netherlands died.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: He had been King of the Netherlands and Grand Duke of Luxembourg for forty-one years.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: But he had no surviving sons, only a ten-year-old daughter, Wilhelmina.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Who became Queen of the Netherlands.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: But in Luxembourg, an old family law, the Nassau family pact, said only men could inherit.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: So the Grand Duchy and the Netherlands, united for seventy-five years, separated.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So who got Luxembourg?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A cousin. A distant one, named Adolphe, the former Duke of Nassau.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: His own duchy in Germany had been swallowed by Prussia in 1866, and he'd been living in exile.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Poor man. Homeless duke.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And now, at the age of seventy-three, he became Grand Duke of Luxembourg.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: For the first time, the country had a ruler who lived there, whose family belonged to it, and who wasn't the king of someone else.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So for the owner count?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Not a new owner. A new family, but the crown stays in the Nassau line.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Fine. A promotion, not a handover.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Still nine.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It was the beginning of the modern Luxembourg monarchy.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Adolphe reigned until 1905. His son William the Fourth followed, and he had no sons, only daughters.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Uh-oh.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: So parliament changed the rules in 1907 to allow women to inherit.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: When William died in 1912, his eldest daughter, Marie-Adélaïde, became Grand Duchess at eighteen.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Eighteen. And the first woman to rule Luxembourg in her own right.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: She was. And in these same years, this tiny country produced a few remarkable people who made their names abroad.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1879, a boy named Edward Steichen was born in the village of Bivange.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: His family emigrated to the United States when he was a toddler, and he grew up to be one of the greatest photographers of the twentieth century.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And he organized a famous exhibition.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The Family of Man, in 1955. It toured the world, and today it is permanently displayed in a castle in the northern town of Clervaux.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Who else?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The physicist Gabriel Lippmann won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1908 for a method of reproducing colors in photographs.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And Hugo Gernsback, born in Luxembourg City in 1884, moved to the United States in 1904 and published some of the first magazines devoted to what he called scientifiction.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Scientifiction. Of course.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: We call it science fiction. The Hugo Awards are named after him.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Wow. A tiny country, and it gave us the Hugo Awards.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: So by 1914, Luxembourg was prosperous, stable, proud, and increasingly sure of its identity.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It had a language its writers loved, a dynasty that was its own, and a fast-growing economy.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: But it still sat between France, Belgium and Germany, and the guarantee of the great powers was only as strong as their promises.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And in the summer of 1914, a crisis in the Balkans pushed Europe toward catastrophe.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The neutrality of Luxembourg was about to be tested.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And I think we know how well that works.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: We do.
